title: Tara and Sprig's Fair Test
markdown:
Once upon a time, in a cozy cottage beside a whispering willow, lived Tara, whose mind was as sharp as her sparkly magnifying glass, and Sprig, a cheerful frog whose giggle bubbled like a clear stream. Tara loved numbers and patterns, and she kept them in a little notebook. Sprig loved to hop, splash, and try new things, even when they did not work the first time.

They were both very excited, because the annual Whispering Willow Racing Seed Competition was just around the corner: a grand event where gardeners from all over showed off their fastest-growing seeds.

Tara had planted her prize seeds in three pots. Sprig had done the same. A sad sight met them. None of the seeds were sprouting well. They looked droopy, like wilted flowers.

“Oh dear,” croaked Sprig, his bright green a little grey. “My racing seeds look more like snoozing seeds. They’re hardly even wiggling.”

Tara tapped her chin with the magnifying glass. “Mine too. They’re supposed to shoot up like little green rockets. They’re sitting there looking sleepy.”

Kindly Dr Kellan ambled over from next door. He was a wise old botanist, and his beard always smelled of damp earth and sunshine. “Trouble with the sprouts? The secret to racing seeds is finding the right conditions. Why not have a little competition between yourselves? Each of you try to make a seed grow its very best — but change only one thing at a time, so you can see what helps the most.”

It sounded like a grand adventure. They each took three pots of their slowest seeds and scurried off. Tara decided to experiment with water: one pot a lot, one pot a little, one pot none. Sprig tested light: one pot in bright sunshine, one in dappled shade, one in a dark quiet corner. They hoped this would quickly show them what the seeds needed to zoom.

After a few days, things were more confusing than before. Tara’s well-watered seed was soggy and sickly yellow. The little-water pot looked better, but sluggish. The no-water seed was a tiny forgotten twig, dry as dust. Sprig’s sunshine seed was wilting, leaves drooping. The shade seed looked all right, but not exciting. The dark-corner seed was pale and spindly, stretching weakly.

Tara flipped through her notebook. The neat rows had gone jumbled. “We changed the water, and you changed the sun, and nothing is clear. We don’t know what helped or what hurt.”

Sprig bounced on his lily pad. “My seeds are all muddled! They don’t know if they want to be sunny or shady, or how much they should drink.”

Dr Kellan chuckled, a warm rumble that made the willow leaves rustle. “When you change too many things at once, it is like trying to hear a whisper in a thunderstorm. You cannot tell what matters.”

Tara looked at her sad seeds, then at Sprig’s confused sprouts. She heard his words again: change only one thing at a time. They had each changed something, but not in a way that let one cause stand still while they watched.

“Wait.” Her voice found a new idea and held it up to the light. “We need to be much more careful. We need a fair test.”

She chose three identical pots. “First, the sun. All three get the exact same amount of water.” She measured. “This one in soft dappled shade. This one more direct sun. This one the brightest sunshine.”

Sprig hopped closer, froggy eyes wide. “So you’re only changing the sun, and keeping the water the same for all of them?”

“Exactly. Then we can see what the sun does by itself. After that, another fair test: change the water a little for each pot, and keep the sunlight the same.”

For the next few days they were incredibly careful. One thing, and only one thing, in each experiment. They watched the sunlight test through. Then they started the water test. They took their time. They noted the colour of leaves, the height of stems, how firmly the roots held the soil. Their voices went hushed with concentration, the way people speak in a library of growing things.

Slowly, like a picture coming into focus, a pattern appeared. The seeds that received just enough water and just enough gentle sunlight began to perk. Leaves unfurled, a vibrant healthy green. Stems grew strong and tall, little green dancers reaching for the light. They were starting to look like racing seeds.

“Look, Tara!” Sprig pointed to a shoot racing upward like a tiny green arrow. “Taller than all the others!”

Tara beamed at her notebook, now full of comparisons that actually compared. “We found what helps them grow best. One thing at a time, we could see what made them happy.”

Dr Kellan’s eyes twinkled even more than usual. “When you test like this — changing only one factor, keeping everything else the same — you are doing what scientists call a fair test. It is a very good way to learn how the world works.”

Sprig’s webbed feet tapped the damp earth. “A fair test! That is why my dark-corner seed looked sleepy, and why the bright-sunshine one got too hot and wilted.”

The willow whispered. The thriving pots stood in a careful row, no longer a jumble. Tara did not make a speech about puzzles. She measured the next day’s water, the same for each, and set the shade pot back in the dappled place, and wondered — only wondered — what else might sit still long enough to be seen, if they asked the garden one question at a time.
characters: Tara (a maths detective), Sprig (a frog), Kellan (a botanist)
